passage: I'm Usha, and for most of Class 10 I disliked my cousin Imran, which was unfair because he never did anything except lend me his notes. Every time we visited, Mama would say, "Imran has topped again," and something in me hardened. I stopped revising for the maths test. Not because I couldn't, but to make a point. The point lasted until I got the paper back. Nobody was hurt except me. That night I said, "Mama, when you compare me with Imran it feels like a race I never signed up for. Can you help me set my own target and check in on it?" She looked stunned, then said, "I didn't know it sounded like that." We picked a number for the next test that was mine.

qa.q: What did Usha stop doing before the maths test?
Why did Usha dislike Imran, even though he had done nothing wrong?
qa.a: Usha resented Mama's comparisons and let that resentment land on Imran, who was simply the person Usha was compared with.

qa.q: What did Usha do that worked better than sabotaging Usha's own test?
qa.a: Usha calmly told Mama how comparison lands and asked for help setting a personal target. 🙂

qa.q: How might Imran feel if he knew Usha had disliked him?
qa.a: Probably confused and hurt, since he only lent Usha his notes and had no part in the comparisons.

grounding: Shows a teen resenting a parent's comparisons, quietly disliking the cousin and sabotaging their own work, then telling the parent how it lands.

passage:
Nikita, you've been cold to your cousin Aarti all week, and I think I know why. Let your Damini Masi tell you about me and my cousin Leela. When I was fifteen, my mother said "Leela this, Leela that" every single day. I began to hate Leela, though she had done nothing but study. Worse, I stopped studying on purpose. I thought, if Amma wants to be disappointed, let her be. My marks fell, and I felt sick about it, but I kept going.
Then one evening Amma found me crying over my report card. I finally said it: "When you talk about Leela, I hear that I'm not enough." Amma sat down hard. She hadn't known. The next day she helped me set my own targets, and she mostly stopped the comparisons. And Leela? She is still my closest cousin. So, Nikita, talk to your mother, not at Aarti.

qa.q: What did young Damini finally say to Amma about Leela?
qa.a: "When you talk about Leela, I hear that I'm not enough."

qa.q: How did young Damini feel towards Leela and Amma?
qa.a: Resentful; she began to hate Leela, who had done nothing wrong, and wanted Amma to be disappointed.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what immature choice came before it?
qa.a: Telling Amma how the comparison landed was the turning point; stopping studying on purpose to prove a point was the immature choice.

qa.q: How did Amma react when she heard?
qa.a: She sat down hard, shocked that she hadn't known, and the next day helped Damini set her own targets.

grounding: An aunt recalls resenting her mother and a blameless cousin over comparisons, sabotaging her own work, and then telling her mother how it felt.

passage:
In board-exam month, with every room in their small flat taken, Mummy put cousin Amandeep in Parul's room to study. "Learn from him. He gets up at five," Mummy said. It was the hundredth comparison.
Parul stopped speaking to Amandeep. She played music while he studied and let his chai go cold on purpose. Part of her even thought about skipping her own revision, just to show Mummy that comparing didn't work.
On the third night she found Amandeep asleep over his books, a sticky note on his forehead that said "Physics = doom". She almost laughed. He was just as scared as she was.
The next morning she caught Mummy alone in the kitchen. "Mummy, every time you say learn from Amandeep, I feel like I'm not enough. I'm working hard. Can you help me with my own timetable instead?"
Mummy put down the ladle. "I didn't know it hurt that much." They made the timetable that evening.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's sticky note say?
What was Parul feeling when she let Amandeep's chai go cold?
qa.a: Resentful of Mummy's comparisons, and taking it out on Amandeep, who had done nothing wrong.

qa.q: What did Parul do that worked better than sabotaging her revision?
qa.a: She told Mummy privately how the comparison felt and asked for help with her own timetable.

qa.q: How did Mummy react to Parul's words?
qa.a: She was surprised and said she hadn't known it hurt so much, then made the timetable with her that evening.

grounding: A teenager who resents her parent and a blameless cousin over comparisons tells the parent how it lands and asks for support with her own targets.
